title: Asian Central Banks vs. The Fed: Diverging Policy Paths
abstract: A careful look at how Asian central banks are navigating the Fed's higher-for-longer stance, with a focus on Japan's yield curve and the BoJ's delicate balancing act.
body:
## Introduction

As a former central-bank economist, I have spent much of my career parsing policy statements and watching how markets react. The past year has been a masterclass in divergence. The Federal Reserve has held rates steady at elevated levels, signalling that the fight against inflation is not yet won. Meanwhile, Asian central banks are charting their own courses, often with different priorities. In this newsletter, I want to separate what policymakers have said from what markets have actually done, focusing on the region's two largest economies: Japan and China. I will also touch on the smaller open economies that are often buffeted by the Fed's decisions. My aim is not to predict the next move, but to lay out the landscape as I see it, with all the caveats that entails.

## The Bank of Japan's Delicate Dance

The Bank of Japan (BoJ) remains the outlier among major central banks. While the Fed and the European Central Bank have raised rates aggressively, the BoJ has kept its policy rate at -0.1% and maintained yield curve control (YCC) with a target band of +/- 0.5% for 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yields. This stance is rooted in the BoJ's long-standing battle against deflation and its desire to see sustainable inflation accompanied by wage growth. In recent months, however, the BoJ has subtly adjusted its approach. At its July 2023 meeting, it widened the YCC band to +/- 0.5% from +/- 0.25%, a move that was framed as a technical adjustment to improve market functioning rather than a step toward normalisation. Since then, Governor Kazuo Ueda has repeatedly said that the BoJ will not hesitate to ease further if needed, but also that it will consider exiting ultra-loose policy if inflation becomes sustainably above 2%. Markets, however, have tested the BoJ's resolve. The 10-year JGB yield has repeatedly approached the upper limit of the band, prompting the BoJ to conduct unscheduled bond purchases. In my view, the BoJ is walking a tightrope: it wants to avoid a sharp rise in yields that could derail the economic recovery, but it also wants to avoid being seen as permanently behind the curve. The recent uptick in inflation, driven partly by cost-push factors, has complicated this task. I would not be surprised to see further tweaks to YCC in the coming months, but I would be cautious about calling it a full-blown tightening cycle.

## China's Targeted Easing

In contrast to the BoJ, the People's Bank of China (PBoC) has been easing policy to support a slowing economy. The PBoC cut its one-year loan prime rate (LPR) in August 2023, and has also reduced the reserve requirement ratio (RRR) for banks. These moves are aimed at boosting credit growth and stabilising the property sector, which has been a drag on activity. Unlike the Fed, the PBoC is not primarily concerned with inflation; consumer price inflation in China has been subdued, and producer prices have been falling. Instead, the PBoC is focused on supporting growth and managing financial risks. The challenge for the PBoC is that its easing may not be as effective as in the past, given the high debt levels and weak confidence. Moreover, the interest rate differential with the US has put downward pressure on the yuan. The PBoC has responded by using its daily fixing and other tools to slow the pace of depreciation, but it has allowed the currency to weaken gradually. In my assessment, the PBoC will continue to prioritise domestic objectives over exchange-rate stability, but it will do so cautiously to avoid triggering capital outflows. The recent measures are incremental, and I expect more targeted easing if growth does not pick up.

## The Fed's Shadow Over Emerging Asia

For many emerging Asian economies, the Fed's policy is a key driver of financial conditions. When the Fed raises rates, it tends to strengthen the US dollar and tighten global financial conditions, which can be challenging for countries with high external debt or current-account deficits. This time around, however, many Asian central banks have been more resilient. Countries like Indonesia, the Philippines, and India have raised rates pre-emptively to defend their currencies and anchor inflation expectations. As a result, they have not had to follow the Fed tick-for-tick. For example, Bank Indonesia has kept rates on hold since January 2023, after a series of hikes in 2022. The Philippine central bank has also paused, citing easing inflation. The Reserve Bank of India has been on hold since February 2023. These decisions reflect a careful balancing act: policymakers want to support growth, but they also want to avoid a sharp depreciation of their currencies that could import inflation. In my view, the worst of the Fed-induced pressure may be behind us, but the risk of further volatility remains if the Fed signals a higher-for-longer stance. Markets have priced in a peak in the Fed funds rate, but the timing of cuts is uncertain. Asian central banks will be watching closely.

## Conclusion

Diverging policy paths are nothing new, but the current environment is particularly complex. The BoJ is slowly inching toward normalisation, but it remains far behind the Fed. The PBoC is easing to support growth, but it is constrained by currency concerns. Other Asian central banks are navigating a middle ground, using pre-emptive hikes and then pausing. As an ex-central-bank economist, I am wary of making bold predictions. What I can say is that the divergence is likely to persist as long as the Fed maintains its restrictive stance. The key risk is that a sudden shift in Fed policy or a sharp appreciation of the dollar could force Asian central banks to adjust their plans. For now, I will continue to watch the data and the statements, and try to distinguish between what is said and what is done. That, after all, is the essence of central-bank watching.
